name: CCDC115-related congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG type IIo)
aliases: Congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIo

clinicalPearls: CCDC115-CDG (CDG type IIo) is a disorder of Golgi homeostasis caused by biallelic variants in CCDC115, a putative assembly factor for the vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase).
Impaired acidification of the Golgi and endolysosomal system disturbs pH-sensitive glycosyltransferases, producing a combined N- and O-linked glycosylation defect (a type II CDG pattern).
The hallmark is infantile-onset hepatopathy — hepatosplenomegaly, raised transaminases and alkaline phosphatase, and hypercholesterolaemia — that can progress to liver failure.
A Wilson-disease-like biochemical picture, with low serum caeruloplasmin and abnormal copper handling, is characteristic and a frequent source of diagnostic confusion.
Neurological involvement — hypotonia and psychomotor or developmental delay — is variable and often milder than the liver disease.
It belongs to a group of V-ATPase / Golgi-homeostasis CDGs (with TMEM199-CDG, ATP6AP1-CDG and ATP6AP2-CDG) that share hepatic, lipid and copper abnormalities.
Severity is broad, ranging from relatively mild childhood disease to fatal infantile hepatic failure.
Diagnosis begins with a type II transferrin glycosylation screen (confirmed by molecular testing); there is no specific curative therapy and management is supportive.
reference.pathophysiology: CCDC115-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIo) results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in CCDC115, which encodes coiled-coil domain-containing protein 115, the human homologue of the yeast vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) assembly factor Vma22p. CCDC115 participates in assembly and trafficking of the V-ATPase and in maintaining the acidic luminal pH of the Golgi apparatus and endolysosomal compartment. Correct Golgi acidification is essential for the localisation and activity of pH-sensitive glycosyltransferases and glycosidases; when it is disturbed, both N-linked and O-linked protein glycosylation are impaired, generating a type II CDG pattern on transferrin analysis. The same disturbance of Golgi and endosomal ion homeostasis perturbs copper and lipid handling, accounting for the low caeruloplasmin, abnormal copper metabolism and hypercholesterolaemia that mimic Wilson disease, and it compromises hepatocyte function, underlying the progressive liver disease that dominates the phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Wilson disease (ATP7B) — the closest biochemical mimic
Other Golgi-homeostasis / V-ATPase CDGs: TMEM199-CDG, ATP6AP1-CDG, ATP6AP2-CDG
Other type II congenital disorders of glycosylation (e.g. ATP6V0A2-CDG, COG-related CDG, MAN1B1-CDG)
Other causes of infantile cholestasis, neonatal hepatitis and paediatric liver failure
Lysosomal storage disorders with hepatosplenomegaly (e.g. Niemann-Pick disease, lysosomal acid lipase deficiency)
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and other inherited metabolic liver diseases
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin glycosylation analysis (isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry) demonstrating a type II pattern
A second glycoprotein / O-glycosylation marker (e.g. apolipoprotein C-III) to confirm a combined defect
Molecular genetic testing — CCDC115 sequencing, a CDG or hepatopathy gene panel, or exome sequencing
Liver function tests, synthetic function and coagulation screen, with a fasting lipid profile
Copper studies — serum caeruloplasmin, serum and urinary copper (and hepatic copper if biopsy is performed)
Liver ultrasound / imaging and, where indicated, liver biopsy
Full blood count (thrombocytopenia may occur) and a broader metabolic screen
redFlags: Progressive hepatosplenomegaly or signs of decompensated liver disease with synthetic failure (coagulopathy, hypoalbuminaemia)
Rising transaminases with jaundice suggesting evolving liver failure
Low caeruloplasmin misattributed to Wilson disease and treated with copper chelation without a molecular diagnosis
Bleeding tendency from coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia
Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive in infancy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable: some children have relatively stable disease with developmental delay and manageable liver involvement, whereas others develop progressive hepatic fibrosis and fatal liver failure in infancy or early childhood. Outcome is largely determined by the severity and progression of the hepatopathy.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the low-caeruloplasmin, abnormal-copper picture as Wilson disease and starting chelation instead of pursuing a CDG diagnosis.
Not requesting transferrin glycosylation analysis in unexplained infantile hepatopathy with hypercholesterolaemia.
Assuming a normal newborn screen excludes the condition — congenital disorders of glycosylation are not detected by routine screening.
Omitting O-glycosylation testing, so the combined (type II) nature of the defect is missed.
Attributing the milder neurological features to another cause and overlooking the hepatic-dominant CDG.
